claims.quote: Extraordinary circumstances, reasons of safety. All aircraft operators by order of the federal government essentially were ground stopped.
claims.claim: On the Friday before November 17, the FAA issued a ground stop for all aircraft operators, citing extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: On Friday, November 13, 2026, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at about 3:54 p.m. ET. Its advisory gave the reason as "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety" and said all departing traffic should stay grounded until further notice. Inbound international flights were handled case by case, so not every aircraft was grounded, but the speaker's word "essentially" covers that. The stop lasted about four to five hours, and thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. Officials later said a telecommunications upgrade by a contractor caused the problem, and law enforcement sources said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The speaker's account of the event and its wording matches the record.
verification.what_is_true: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop of all departing flights on Friday, November 13, 2026, citing "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." Officials later blamed an equipment problem during a telecommunications network upgrade.

sources.excerpt: On November 13 at approximately 3:30 p.m. ET, the FAA experienced a technical problem that resulted in issuing a nationwide ground stop.
The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m., pausing all departures across the country. The FAA's alert said the stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."

"All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice," an air traffic control advisory posted Friday afternoon read. "Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis."
Friday's nationwide ground stop started when a contractor updated old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication lines, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

claims.quote: on Friday there was an unscheduled visit to Washington, DC from the director of the Mossad.
claims.claim: The director of Israel's Mossad made an unscheduled visit to Washington, DC on the Friday before November 17.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: Several outlets, citing Axios and three sources familiar with the visit, reported that Mossad Director Roman Gofman was in Washington on Friday, November 13, 2026. He met CIA Director John Ratcliffe and other Trump administration officials about Iran, and was also expected to meet envoy Steve Witkoff in Miami. The trip was not announced in advance. The Mossad, CIA and White House declined to comment, and Ynet called it a "special visit." That fits the word "unscheduled," although no source uses that exact word. Ynet also reported that Gofman returned to Israel on Sunday, November 15, so the co-host's later remark that he was "still" in town on Monday is not supported. The reports also give no evidence connecting the visit to the outages discussed in the episode.
verification.what_is_true: Mossad Director Roman Gofman made a visit to Washington, DC on Friday, November 13, 2026 that had not been announced beforehand. He met CIA Director John Ratcliffe and other Trump administration officials to discuss Iran.

sources.excerpt: Mossad Director Roman Gofman was in Washington on Friday for a meeting about Iran with his CIA counterpart John Ratcliffe, the Axios news site reported, citing three sources with knowledge of the matter.

Mossad Director Roman Gofman returned to Israel on Sunday afternoon following a special visit to the United States, where he briefed senior Trump administration officials and CIA Director John Ratcliffe
Mossad Director Roman Gofman traveled to Washington on Friday for discussions with senior officials in the Trump administration concerning the ongoing confrontation with Iran, Axios reported
Mossad Director Roman Gofman met with senior Trump administration officials in Washington on Friday to discuss the war in Iran
Gofman met with Trump administration officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, in Washington, the people said

claims.quote: the overriding issue was the war in Iran. There's no question about it. Every exit poll said the same thing.
claims.claim: Exit polls from the recent elections showed the war in Iran was the overriding issue for voters, and most voters opposed it.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: I couldn't verify this claim. My search tool hit its usage limit before it returned any results, so I found no exit poll data from the November 2026 elections. That includes the network exit polls and AP VoteCast. Without them, I can't confirm or rule out that the Iran war was the top issue in every exit poll, or that most voters opposed it. The speaker named no poll. In past midterms, exit polls have usually ranked the economy or cost of living first, but that doesn't settle what happened in 2026. A reviewer should check the 2026 network exit polls and AP VoteCast directly.
verification.what_is_true: The speaker said Republicans did badly in the recent elections. Whether that's right, and what exit polls showed about the Iran war, couldn't be checked because no search results came back.

claims.quote: Last Thursday, last Thursday, so that's November 12th, just a few days ago. It's only November 17th here, right? Last Thursday we got this headline, Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage.
claims.claim: On Thursday, November 12, Microsoft reported identifying issues behind a global Outlook outage.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: A large Microsoft 365 outage began on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and mainly hit Outlook and Exchange Online. Microsoft gave updates that day, saying the problem appeared to come from servers being unavailable and that there was no sign of malicious activity. The claim gets one detail wrong. The exact headline the speaker quotes, ABC News' "Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage," ran on Monday, November 16. It covered a Microsoft executive's later post explaining the cause, which was a "latent defect," increased load and reduced server capacity. Microsoft did give a cause on the day of the outage, but the quoted headline came four days later. That date error doesn't change the main point.
verification.what_is_true: A global Outlook/Microsoft 365 outage began on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and Microsoft gave preliminary explanations that day. A fuller account of the cause, carried under the quoted headline, was published on November 16.

sources.excerpt: Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage... November 16, 2026, 9:26 AM... In a lengthy social media post Monday morning, a Microsoft executive said a combination of a "latent defect," increased load and lessened server capacity...
Updates throughout the day on Thursday indicated the company believed the issue may have stemmed from an issue with server availability.
The Microsoft Outlook outage that started on November 12, 2026, began as an Exchange Online mailbox access problem in the Americas and widened into a global Microsoft 365 service degradation.
Nov 13, 2026, 1:48 AM GMT Microsoft reveals cause of massive service outage

claims.quote: Just a couple of weeks ago, the Republicans got their butts kicked in the elections, absolutely annihilated.
claims.claim: Republicans suffered major losses in elections held a couple of weeks before November 17.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: The midterm elections were held on November 3, 2026, two weeks before the episode was recorded on November 17. Major outlets reported that Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate. Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most in nearly 70 years, giving them a 56–44 majority. They also won roughly 250 or more House seats and flipped several governorships and state legislative chambers. CNBC noted that Republicans had not flipped a single seat held by Democrats. Coverage commonly called the result a 'rout' and a 'drubbing,' which matches the speaker's description. This check covers only the claim about the size of the loss. It does not cover the speaker's separate statement about exit polls and the Iran war.
verification.what_is_true: In the November 3, 2026 midterms, Republicans lost both chambers of Congress by large margins, and Democrats made broad gains at the state level, so 'annihilated' is a fair description of the scale.

sources.excerpt: Democrats have flipped seven Senate seats, nearly 30 House districts, five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers in a historic 2026 midterm rout.
Donald Trump's Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in a stinging rebuke from voters.
Democrats officially flipped their ninth U.S. Senate seat of the 2026 midterm elections — the most in nearly 70 years.
Recap: Vance blames Iran war for GOP losses as Democrats retake Congress

claims.quote: Workday outage locked employees and firms out of pay and benefits on a Friday.
claims.claim: An outage at HR and payroll company Workday on a Friday locked employees and firms out of pay and benefits systems.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: Several outlets reported that Workday had a widespread outage starting Friday evening, November 13, 2026. Employees at client organizations could not log in, clock in or out, view pay information, request time off or enroll in benefits. Workday serves roughly 11,500 organizations, and reported customers include Target, Walmart, Charles Schwab and NASA's JPL. Workday said a disaster-recovery test had left production data inconsistent, and it told the AP the outage was not a security incident. Service was restored on November 14. The reports describe lost access to pay information and benefits systems. They don't confirm that paychecks were missed, as the speaker suggested later in the segment. Still, the claim as quoted matches the reporting.
verification.what_is_true: On Friday, November 13, 2026, a Workday outage left employees at many client firms unable to access pay information, timekeeping and benefits enrollment until service came back on November 14. Workday blamed a failed disaster-recovery test.

sources.excerpt: A widespread Workday outage on the evening of November 13 left employees unable to clock in and out, access their pay info, request for time off or file for benefits.

sources.publisher: San Francisco Chronicle via Yahoo Tech
sources.excerpt: Workday, the Bay Area payroll and human resources tech giant, experienced an outage Friday, with some employees unable to access their workplace accounts or complete tasks.
Workday outage left thousands of companies without access to payroll and HR software Friday, joining Microsoft in experiencing a major service disruption this week.
Workday went into maintenance Friday after a disaster-recovery test left production data inconsistent.
Workday told the Associated Press the outage was not related to a security incident.

claims.quote: Major banking outage linked to Chase impacted Wells Fargo and Bank of America.
claims.claim: A major banking outage linked to Chase affected Wells Fargo and Bank of America customers on the Monday in question.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: On Monday, November 16, 2026, JPMorgan Chase had a nationwide outage that it blamed on a software bug in on-premise hardware. Chase said it was not a cyberattack. ABC7 and Al Jazeera reported that Wells Fargo and Bank of America customers also had problems, mainly when sending money to or receiving it from Chase, including through Zelle. Downdetector logged spikes in complaints for both banks. Bank of America said its own systems ran normally, and Chase said the problem was not systemic. Fortune said it was unclear whether Wells Fargo's online banking trouble had the same cause as Chase's. Even so, the claim as worded, that a Chase-linked outage affected customers at both banks, matches the reporting.
verification.what_is_true: On November 16, 2026, a Chase software bug disrupted transactions. The disruption spilled over to customers at Wells Fargo, Bank of America and other banks who were trying to complete transactions with Chase. Bank of America said its own systems were not down, and Chase called it a Chase-only, non-cyber issue.

sources.excerpt: People at other banks, like Wells Fargo and Bank of America, had problems as they were trying to complete transactions with Chase through Zelle.

Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments.
Bank of America told Fortune... systems were operating normally... it was not clear whether the Chase and Wells Fargo failures shared a cause.

claims.quote: Popular websites subverted in bid to steal crypto. And target iPhone users. These are some of the world's most viewed websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC— that's a bank— Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA.
claims.claim: Reuters reported that popular websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, were subverted to steal cryptocurrency and target iPhone users.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: A Reuters story dated Nov. 16, 2026 ran under the headline the speaker quoted. It named Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA and said malicious JavaScript reached visitors to the websites of 178 organizations through the website optimization platform Optimizely. The speaker's details match the report. The account came from security researcher Scott Helme. Reuters said it could not immediately confirm whether the code was successfully used in each case or how far any resulting hacks went. In the podcast, the item was grouped with a series of service outages, but the Reuters report describes a supply-chain script compromise, not a site outage.
verification.what_is_true: Reuters reported on Nov. 16, 2026 that a security researcher said websites of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, IKEA and others (178 organizations in all) were subverted through Optimizely scripts to steal cryptocurrency and target iPhones. Reuters noted that the extent of any successful hacks was not yet confirmed.

sources.excerpt: Some of the world's most visited websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, were subverted in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, a security researcher said on Monday.

Malicious JavaScript was aimed at visitors to the websites of 178 organizations across various sectors through Optimizely... Reuters could not immediately ascertain whether the code was successfully used in each case.

Nov 16 (Reuters) - Some of the world's most visited websites, including those belonging to Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, were subverted in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones.

claims.quote: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down. Sources say this is a network communication system used within the NSA, and there were 6 people cited.
claims.claim: CNN reported, citing six sources, that NSANet, a highly classified NSA internal communications network, went down.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: CNN published an exclusive on November 17, 2026, headlined "Highly classified US national security communications network goes down." It cited six people familiar with the matter and said the network, NSANet, is used for the NSA's internal communications. It also reported that sources saw no evidence of a cyberattack at that point. Other outlets, including the Detroit News, Israel Hayom and the Jerusalem Post, credited CNN and repeated the six-source detail. That matches the co-host's description. Later reports said NSA officials described the problem as a temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance, and some outlets linked it to software patching. Those later details don't change whether the co-host described CNN's report correctly.
verification.what_is_true: On November 17, 2026, CNN reported, citing six people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the highly classified network the NSA uses for internal communications, was down, and that sources saw no evidence of a cyberattack.

sources.excerpt: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. … At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
CNN, which first reported on the outage, said that it affected NSANet, which allows employees to share classified information internally.
A highly classified communications network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) has gone down, CNN reported Tuesday, citing six people familiar with the matter.
A different U.S. official said that the NSA "experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance."

claims.quote: The FBI says RTX AI open-source hacking tool has been used to breach networks in under 3 hours.
claims.claim: TechCrunch reported that the FBI said an open-source AI hacking tool called RTX has been used to breach networks in under three hours.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: On November 16, 2026, TechCrunch ran the headline "FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours.'" "RTX" in the transcript is almost certainly a mistranscription of "Artex" (styled ARTEX). The article was based on an FBI FLASH advisory dated November 13. It said Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours" in some cases. The quote matches what was reported. Two details add context: the three-hour figure describes some cases, not all, and the developer has since made the tool closed-source, though the FBI says the older open-source version still circulates. None of these reports ties Artex to the outages discussed earlier in the episode.
verification.what_is_true: TechCrunch reported that an FBI flash advisory warned that hackers used Artex, an open-source AI penetration-testing tool, to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to breaches at ConnectWise, Barracuda and South Korean banks.

sources.excerpt: In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours."
The FBI is warning that hackers are using an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against organizations worldwide
The FBI's November 13 flash advisory identifies ARTEX, an open-source, large language model-driven agentic platform, as a tool used by malicious actors to automate multiple stages of cyber intrusions
Artex has been tied to breaches at ConnectWise, Barracuda and South Korean banks

claims.quote: Last Thursday, last Thursday, so that's November 12th, just a few days ago. It's only November 17th here, right? Last Thursday we got this headline, Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage.
claims.claim: On Thursday, November 12, Microsoft reported a global Outlook outage that also affected other Microsoft services such as Teams and Word.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: A major global Microsoft 365 outage began on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Outlook, Teams and Copilot were all affected, and Microsoft reported the problem and apologized. The outage ran into November 13–14 and spanned two workdays. One detail is off: the headline the speaker quoted, "Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage," was an ABC News story from Monday, November 16. It was not a Thursday headline. That story covered Microsoft's root-cause explanation, a latent software defect. Microsoft also said Teams chats and meetings worked normally for most of the outage, and that Office apps recovered earlier than email. The speaker's later remark that nobody had an explanation is outside this claim. Microsoft did publicly say the outage was not a cyberattack.
verification.what_is_true: A global Microsoft 365 outage hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other services starting Thursday, November 12, 2026, and Microsoft publicly acknowledged it. The quoted headline came later, on November 16, when Microsoft explained the cause.

sources.excerpt: Microsoft identifies issues leading to global Outlook outage... November 16, 2026... a combination of a 'latent defect,' increased load and lessened server capacity
triggered a chain reaction during peak U.S. business hours Nov. 12... Teams chats and meetings worked normally for most of the outage... 'This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling'
Microsoft is investigating a widespread outage affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams, and Copilot... November 12, 2026
A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.
A major global Microsoft outage occurred from November 12 to 14, 2026. Problems were reported with numerous Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot.

claims.quote: we get a headline about the FAA ground stop. And when you look at it, it's a pretty crazily worded message. Extraordinary circumstances, reasons of safety. All aircraft operators by order of the federal government essentially were ground stopped.
claims.claim: On the Friday after the Microsoft outage, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop citing extraordinary circumstances and safety reasons, later attributed to a routine upgrade that went awry.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: I couldn't verify this claim. My web searches failed because the search tool hit its usage limit and returned no usable results. So I couldn't find any FAA statement, ground-stop notice or news report confirming a nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, 2026. I also couldn't confirm the wording of the notice the speaker described ("extraordinary circumstances," "reasons of safety") or that the stop was later blamed on an upgrade that went wrong. The FAA has ordered nationwide ground stops before, including in January 2023 after a failure in its NOTAM system, but that doesn't confirm this event. A reviewer should check FAA advisories and news coverage from November 13–17, 2026.
verification.what_is_true: The FAA has the authority to order nationwide ground stops and has done so before, such as during the NOTAM system outage in January 2023. I found no evidence either confirming or contradicting the specific November 2026 ground stop or the reason the speaker says was given for it.

claims.quote: We get this tweet from United Airlines. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage.
claims.claim: United Airlines posted on Monday that it was aware of a widespread system outage, and said there was no indication it was due to cybersecurity-related issues.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: On Monday, November 16, 2026, United Airlines replied to a customer on X. The post said: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage," and added that its teams were working to restore service. The co-host's reading matches the post. United later said the outage was resolved after about 90 minutes and that there was "no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue." CNN, CBS, ABC, CNBC and NBC Chicago all reported that statement. The podcast's paraphrase is a little garbled: it says "no indication this is any kind of an outage." But the substance of the claim, the X post and the denial of a cybersecurity cause, is correct.
verification.what_is_true: United posted on X on November 16, 2026, that it was aware of a widespread system outage, using the words quoted on the podcast. It later said there was no indication the outage was cybersecurity-related. The outage delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes.

sources.excerpt: We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible.
"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage..." United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer.
United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue.
There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.
The outage lasted about 90 minutes. … A United spokesperson said there's no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity issue.

claims.quote: You've not been listening to Bill Gates, the guy who flew to the island all the time. You've not been listening to Bill Gates, the guy whose wife left him because he flew to the island.
claims.claim: Bill Gates frequently flew to Jeffrey Epstein's island, and his wife divorced him because of it.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates ever visited Jeffrey Epstein's private island, much less often. The flight logs that have been made public show him on Epstein's plane once, in March 2013, flying from Teterboro, New Jersey, to Palm Beach, Florida. FactCheck.org found earlier viral claims of repeated island trips baseless. The DOJ's 2026 document release and Gates's June 2026 House Oversight interview showed that Epstein invited him to the island, but there was no sign he accepted, and Gates said he never went. Melinda French Gates has said his ties to Epstein were one of several reasons for the divorce. Their meetings, not island trips, are what she pointed to.
verification.what_is_true: Gates met Epstein several times starting in 2011, flew on Epstein's plane once in 2013, and later called the relationship a mistake. Melinda French Gates has said his ties to Epstein were one factor in her decision to end their marriage.

sources.excerpt: There's no evidence that Bill Gates ever visited Jeffrey Epstein's private island in the Caribbean... The March 2013 flight actually went from Teterboro Airport, in New Jersey, to Palm Beach International Airport in Florida.
Gates has maintained he never visited the island and there's no indication he accepted the invite.
The disgraced financier invited Gates to his island several times but Gates declined, according to the transcript.
French Gates has previously said that her ex-husband's association with Epstein was one factor of many that led her to seek divorce.
Melinda French Gates suggested Bill Gates' ties to Epstein contributed to divorce

claims.quote: The Director of National Intelligence comes out, a guy named Jay Clayton. The Director of National Intelligence comes out and says, also, no evidence of cyberattack here.
claims.claim: Jay Clayton, identified as the Director of National Intelligence, stated there was no evidence of a cyberattack behind the outages.
claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: My web searches failed, so I couldn't check what officials said about the November 2026 outages. From background knowledge I can't confirm here, Jay Clayton chaired the SEC from 2017 to 2020 and became U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York in 2025. He was not Director of National Intelligence; Tulsi Gabbard was confirmed to that post in February 2025. If that was still true in November 2026, calling Clayton the DNI is probably wrong. However, I can't rule out a later change in the post, and I couldn't check whether Clayton, the DNI or another official said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. A reviewer should check this with sources.
verification.what_is_true: Based on my background knowledge, Jay Clayton is a real federal official, a former SEC chair who became U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York in 2025. He was not the Director of National Intelligence as of 2025. I couldn't confirm any statement from him about the outages.

claims.quote: We, we do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack. Let me just be, be clear about that. And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.
claims.claim: A US official stated the government did not see signs of a coordinated cyberattack or state-sponsored activity behind the outages.
claims.speaker: E
claims.speaker_name: Jay Clayton (identified by Speaker B as Director of National Intelligence)

verification.explanation: Several outlets and a White House release report that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said this in a Fox Business interview on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The White House quoted him word for word. He said officials saw no indicia of a coordinated cyberattack or of state-sponsored activity. Instead, he blamed the outages on institutions patching vulnerabilities and upgrading systems. On November 18, he repeated the point in testimony to the House Homeland Security Committee, where he said the outages were not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack. The claim correctly reflects what the official said. Whether his assessment is correct is a separate question that this check does not settle.
verification.what_is_true: Jay Clayton, the US Director of National Intelligence, publicly said in November 2026 that officials did not see signs of a coordinated cyberattack or state-sponsored activity behind the wave of tech outages. He attributed the outages to patching and system upgrades.

sources.excerpt: DNI Clayton: "We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here."

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday that officials see no signs of a coordinated cyberattack or state-sponsored activity behind a wave of technology outages, pointing instead to institutions installing security patches.
Recent outages in the U.S. do not represent a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said at a hearing on Wednesday.
And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here. And we can be fairly confident in that," Clayton said.

claims.quote: Lots of institutions, because these vulnerabilities have been identified, are patching. They're taking their systems down. They're upgrading them.
claims.claim: The official stated that the outages resulted from many institutions patching and upgrading systems after vulnerabilities were identified, with some systems failing to come back as expected.
claims.speaker: E
claims.speaker_name: Jay Clayton (identified by Speaker B as Director of National Intelligence)

verification.explanation: The claim is about what DNI Jay Clayton said, and the record backs it up. The White House published a transcript on November 18, 2026, quoting him saying that "lots of institutions" were patching newly identified vulnerabilities and taking systems down to upgrade them. In the same remarks he said some systems were "not coming back as expected in all cases," and handoffs between systems were failing too. Fox Business, ABC News, Quartz and Nextgov reported the same explanation. Clayton was sworn in as DNI in August 2026, so the speaker is identified correctly. This check only confirms that he made the statement. It doesn't independently confirm what actually caused the outages, though Nextgov reported that officials gave Congress the same account.
verification.what_is_true: DNI Jay Clayton publicly said the November 2026 outages came from institutions patching and upgrading systems after vulnerabilities were found, and that some systems did not come back online as expected. He also said there was no sign of a coordinated or state-sponsored cyberattack.

sources.excerpt: Lots of institutions, because these vulnerabilities have been identified, are patching. They're taking their systems down, they're upgrading them... they're not coming back as expected in all cases.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says security patches after a PHP vulnerability caused system outages
They said companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems caused them, according to the White House.

claims.quote: The expert testified at the preliminary hearing and produced a report that she was unable to determine whether that bullet was fired from that particular rifle.

claims.speaker: B
claims.speaker_name: Unknown (co-host filling in; refers to 'Candace and I')

verification.explanation: The substance is correct. At Tyler Robinson's July 2026 preliminary hearing, the defense called the firearms examiner who wrote the lab report. She testified that the bullet jacket fragment recovered from Charlie Kirk's body could not be identified as fired from the recovered rifle, nor excluded. She said this was because the fragment had too few microscopic marks. One detail is wrong: the examiner, Samantha Karner, works for the ATF, not the FBI. The FBI took custody of the rifle and sent it to the ATF lab for testing. Her report also found that a cartridge case was fired from that rifle. Her result on the fragment was inconclusive. It did not mean the bullet failed to match the rifle.
verification.what_is_true: The examiner, a woman, testified at the preliminary hearing, and her report said the bullet jacket fragment 'could not be identified or excluded' as fired from the rifle. She works for the ATF, not the FBI.
